routes.label: Bound the remaining value at consecutive years

question: Suppose that at the end of any year, a unit of money has lost \(10\%\) of the value it had at the beginning of that year. Find the smallest integer \(n\) such that after \(n\) years the unit of money will have lost at least \(90\%\) of its value. (To the nearest thousandth \(\log_{10}3\) is \(0.477.\))
solution:
Each year the money retains \(90\%\) of its previous value. Measured as a fraction of its original value, the amount remaining after \(n\) years is
\[
v_n=\left(\frac9{10}\right)^n.
\]
Losing at least \(90\%\) means \(v_n\le1/10\). To find the first qualifying year, we can compare the remaining values at consecutive years using exact bounds.

Squaring \((0.9)^5=0.59049\) gives
\[
\frac13<(0.9)^{10}=0.3486784401<\frac7{20}.
\]
The lower bound shows that after \(21\) years,
\[
(0.9)^{21}
=\frac9{10}\bigl((0.9)^{10}\bigr)^2
>\frac9{10}\left(\frac13\right)^2
=\frac1{10}.
\]
The upper bound shows that after \(22\) years,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(0.9)^{22}
&=\frac{81}{100}\bigl((0.9)^{10}\bigr)^2\\
&<\frac{81}{100}\left(\frac7{20}\right)^2
=\frac{3969}{40000}
<\frac1{10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining value decreases every year because it is multiplied by \(9/10\). Thus every year through \(21\) fails the requirement, while year \(22\) satisfies it. The smallest integer is \(22\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).

The formula a_n equals a1 times q to n minus one uses the initial term and common ratio of a geometric sequence.

The closed form a1*q^(n-1) is one compact route. Repeatedly multiplying the current amount by the fixed factor computes a permitted finite future quantity without forming or evaluating that general-term formula. Claude identifies the same resulting sequence value but does not establish necessity of the particular procedure; retain the named method component.
